Jandarma ve Sahil Güvenlik Akademisi Başkanlığı, Jandarma Genel Komutanlığı bünyesinde görevlendirilmek üzere 9 bin uzman erbaş alımı yapılacağını duyurdu.
Resmi Gazete'de yayımlanan ilanla birlikte alım yapılacak kadrolar ve başvuru takvimi de netleşti. Duyurunun ardından Jandarma Genel Komutanlığına katılmak isteyen adaylar, başvuru şartlarını ve alım sürecinin ayrıntılarını araştırmaya başladı.
Yayımlanan ilana göre, Jandarma Genel Komutanlığına toplam 9 bin erkek uzman erbaş alınacak. Alım kapsamında en yüksek kontenjan jandarma branşına ayrılırken farklı uzmanlık alanlarında da personel istihdam edilecek.
10 havacılık personeli (5 uçak/helikopter teknisyen yardımcısı, 5 havacılık itfaiyecisi)
Jandarma Genel Komutanlığı 9 bin uzman erbaş alımı için başvurular 23 Kasım 2026 tarihinde başladı. Adaylar, başvurularını 7 Aralık 2026 saat 23.59'a kadar tamamlayabilecek.
Başvurular, Jandarma ve Sahil Güvenlik Akademisi Başkanlığı Personel Temin Sistemi üzerinden alınacak. Adayların https://personeltemin.jandarma.gov.tr adresine girerek e-Devlet aracılığıyla başvuru işlemlerini gerçekleştirmesi gerekiyor.
Alıma ilişkin yaş, eğitim, sağlık ve diğer başvuru koşulları ile değerlendirme aşamalarına dair ayrıntılar, Jandarma Genel Komutanlığı tarafından yayımlanan 2027 Yılı Jandarma Genel Komutanlığı Uzman Erbaş Temini Kılavuzu içerisinde yer alıyor.
Adaylar, başvuru şartları ve alım sürecine ilişkin güncel bilgilere Jandarma Genel Komutanlığının www.jandarma.gov.tr, Jandarma ve Sahil Güvenlik Akademisinin www.jsga.edu.tr ve Kamu İlan sayfasının https://kamuilan.sbb.gov.tr adreslerinden ulaşabiliyor.

Programın on beşinci haftasında eleme potasında Şükran, Tolgahan, Şadi ve Armağan yer aldı. Şükran haftanın ilk eleme adayı olmuştu. Cumartesi akşamı oynanan son dokunulmazlık oyununda takım kaptanı olan Şükran, eşit biten oylamada son sözü söyleyerek Armağan'ı potaya göndermişti.

TV8 ekranlarının sevilen yarışması MasterChef Türkiye'de haftanın eleme gecesi geride kaldı. 22 Kasım Pazar günü yayınlanan bölümde eleme potasındaki dört yarışmacı, Danilo Zanna, Mehmet Yalçınkaya ve Somer Sivrioğlu'nun karşısında hünerlerini sergiledi. İki aşamalı mücadelenin sonunda en düşük puanı alan yarışmacı, MasterChef hayallerine veda etti. İşte MasterChef'e veda eden isim...
Eleme gecesinin ilk etabında Şadi, Şükran, Armağan ve Tolgahan'dan ana malzeme olarak yer elması kullanarak yaratıcı yemekler hazırlamaları istendi. Şeflerin verdiği 45 dakikalık sürenin ardından yarışmacılar tabaklarını değerlendirmeye sundu.
İlk turun puan sıralamasında Armağan 21,5 puanla zirveye yerleşti. Şükran 21 puanla ikinci, Şadi 20,5 puanla üçüncü, Tolgahan ise 17,5 puanla dördüncü sırada yer aldı.
İlk turun ardından eleme heyecanı ikinci etapla devam etti. Yarışmacılar bu kez Somer Şef'in "Ben Saksı Değilim" adlı tabağını hazırlamak için tezgah başına geçti. Şeflerin verdiği bir saatlik sürenin sonunda tabaklar yeniden puanlandı.
Değerlendirme sonucunda Armağan ve Şadi eleme potasından kurtulurken gecenin son iki yarışmacısı Şükran ve Tolgahan oldu.
Şeflerin iki etapta verdiği puanların toplamı sonucunda MasterChef Türkiye'ye veda eden yarışmacı Şükran oldu. Tolgahan, rakibinden 1 puan fazla alarak ilk 11'e kalmayı başardı.
Tabağını tamamlayamadığı için büyük üzüntü yaşayan Şükran, elenmesinin ardından gözyaşlarını tutamadı. Böylece MasterChef Türkiye'de 22 Kasım Pazar akşamının eleme gecesi sona erdi.
Şükran, ''Şimdi gideceğimi bilsem bile gene aynı şeyi yapardım. Takım arkadaşlarımla yarışırken aldığım karar gerçekten onların düzeni bozulmasın. Biz küçük toplumda büyüdük. Aman düzen bozulmasın mantığıyla büyüdüğümüz için o niyetleydim. Nasip devreye giriyor. Ben burada çok güzel şeyler yaşadım. Oğluma hatıra bırakmak için gelmiştim. Seyircilerden bir yanlışım olduysa özür dilerim.'' diye belirtti.
Gözyaşlarına hakim olamayan Şükran, ''Onu çok özledim. Ben evde kendimi motive etmek için örgü örüyordum. Hepinize birer tane atkı ördüm. Bugün de o kadar emindim ki kendimden yoksa yanımda getirirdim. O bana terapi oluyordu. Sizleri tanıdığıma çok memnunum oğluma hatıra bıraktım. Burnumun direği sızlıyor. Anneciğim, ben buraya sadece senin için geldim. Sana güzel bir hatıra bırakmak için geldim. İyi ya da kötü bir sürü olaylar yaşadım ama hayatım boyunca tek yapman gereken şey her zaman dürüst olman ve inandığın yolda hep devam etmen yavrucuğum. Bunu izlediğinde umarım çok mutlu olursun'' diye ekledi.

John Kennedy looks to Trump leaders as he asks how China evidently bypassed export controls for Nvidia’s top AI chips
Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang ’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.
The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, where the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China.
On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union , the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.
He also said on Fox News Sunday: “There are chips that have ended up in places that they should not.”
Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick , and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”.
“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said.
Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it.
Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders are either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”.
He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”.
“And if secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said.
Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company.
“It behooves Nvidia to move ⁠quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program.
Kennedy, a former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl.
Many believe Kennedy resorts to the drawl to come off as folksy – while he holds degrees from Vanderbilt University, the University of Virginia School of Law and the UK’s Oxford University, and is estimated to be one of the wealthiest US senators.

ABD'de 3 Kasım'daki ara seçimlerin ardından hâlâ dört sandalyenin kazananı belirsiz. Ancak şimdiye kadarki sonuçlar Demokratlar için 1992'den beri en büyük zafer anlamına geliyor.
ABD'de 3 Kasım'daki ara seçimlerin ardından oy sayım ve itiraz süreçleri devam ediyor.
Son olarak Kuzey Carolina'da Demokrat aday Chuck Hubbard'ın Cumhuriyetçi temsilci Virginia Foxx'u mağlup ederek Temsilciler Meclisine girdiği duyuruldu.
Demokratlar bu sonuçla, 435 sandalyeli Temsilciler Meclisine 258 üye göndermeyi başardı. Böylece son 34 yılın en büyük çoğunluğunu elde etmiş oldular.
Sonuç, Foxx'un yeniden sayım talebinde bulunmasının ardından kesinleşti.
Hubbard, Foxx ile görüştüğünü belirterek, "Yeniden sayımın ardından kendisi büyük bir nezaketle yenilgiyi kabul etti" dedi.
Temsilciler Meclisinde Ocak ayında yeni dönemin başlamasıyla, Bill Clinton'ın başkan seçildiği 1992'den bu yana herhangi bir partinin ulaştığı en büyük çoğunluk kurulmuş olacak.
Demokratların önde gelen ismi Hakeem Jeffries gelişmeyi, "Demokratlar, bu yüzyılda Kongrede herhangi bir partinin elde ettiği en büyük çoğunluğu az önce garantiledi" ifadesiyle değerlendirdi.
Temsilciler Meclisinde hâlâ sonucun kesinleşmediği dört sandalye bulunuyor.
Senato yarışı ise 44'e karşı 56 ile yine Demokratların açık üstünlüğü ile tamamlandı. Teksas, Kansas, Mississippi ve Alaska gibi Cumhuriyetçilerin "kale" olarak gördüğü önemli eyaletler Demokratlara geçti.
Demokratlar hem Temsilciler Meclisi hem de Senato'nun kontrolünü tamamen ele geçirirken , Cumhuriyetçiler çok sayıda sürpriz yenilgi aldı.
Sonuçlar ABD Başkanı Donald Trump'ın politikalarına yönelik ağır bir tepki olarak görülüyor.
Hayat pahalılığı, gümrük tarifeleri ve İran savaşı Amerikalıların hoşnutsuzluğunun temel sebepleri. "Savaşları bitirme" sözüyle seçilen Trump'ın başlattığı İran savaşı, tüm dünyada olduğu gibi ABD'de de akaryakıt fiyatlarının hızla yükselmesine yol açtı.
Kongre çoğunluğu Ocak ayından itibaren Demokratlara, kalan iki yılında Trump'ın politikalarını engelleme ve yolsuzluk iddialarını soruşturma olanacağı sağlayacak.

Exclusive: Statement on death of Australian music industry legend drafted using search and AI but ‘fact checked and edited’ before approval, party says
Tributes flow for Molly Meldrum: Human Nature, Jason Donovan and others remember music industry great
A statement on the death of Molly Meldrum attributed to the Victorian opposition leader, Jess Wilson , was written using AI, the Liberal party has confirmed.
Meldrum, the Australian music journalist, broadcaster and producer, died on Monday morning . He was 83. Shortly after his death, Wilson issued a statement describing Meldrum as a “true Australian icon who will never be forgotten”.
“His famous cowboy hat, his larger-than-life personality and his lifelong love for his beloved Saints made him unmistakably Molly,” the statement read.
“But above all, he will be remembered for his generosity, his warmth and the enormous affection Australians held for him.”
When submitted to AI-detector service Pangram, the 177-word statement came up as 100% AI-authored. Pangram maintains its algorithm is so accurate that it incorrectly identifies text as an AI output only about one in every 10,000 times.
In response to questions from Guardian Australia, a Liberal party spokesperson confirmed the party used AI to compile research on Meldrum’s career and draft the statement.
“Like plenty of workplaces, we use search and AI to help with drafting and researching a variety of material, which was the case here,” the spokesperson said.
“The initial draft was done using a combination of search and AI to compile Molly’s extensive career.”
It is understood the initial AI-generated draft did not include references to Meldrum’s time on TV variety show, Hey Hey It’s Saturday or the two times he was crowned as the king of Melbourne’s Moomba festival. That information was added by a member of the team.
“The statement was then fact checked and edited by a member of the team before it was provided to the Leader for approval,” the spokesperson said. “The final version pays tribute to a true legend of the Australian entertainment industry.”
A tribute by the premier, Ben Carroll, came up as 100% human-authored when submitted to Pangram.
In it, the Victorian Labor leader described the Sunday night tradition of tuning into Meldrum’s Countdown program and then heading to a record shop on Monday morning to ask for the song he recommended.
This article includes content provided by Instagram . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue' .
“Molly gave young Australian musicians a chance to be heard in lounge rooms across the country,” Carroll’s statement said.
“Years before Countdown, he helped start the St Kilda cheer squad. Supporting others was in his nature. A giant of the Australian music industry and a true character.”
Carroll said Meldrum would be honoured with a state funeral.
AI has been used extensively during the Victorian election campaign by the major parties and One Nation, as well as third-party campaigners. Labor’s release of a deepfake video of Wilson trick-or-treating alongside One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, was widely criticised and prompted the Greens to call for the practice to be banned altogether.
Timothy Koskie, a media researcher at the University of Sydney, said authenticity is becoming a “harder currency to build” due to the prevalence of AI.
“The public is doubting the credibility, authenticity, reliability of just about everything in the shared social space,” he said.
Last month, the Australian Electoral Commissioner, Jeff Pope, told the federal parliamentary inquiry on artificial intelligence that there would be challenges in requiring political communications to be labelled if AI was used in its creation.
“The challenge with that is that, if AI is not already ubiquitous, it’s not far away,” he said. “If you’re labelling everything with AI, then, at the next election or not too long thereafter, every bit of political communication could have an AI label on it, and you’ve got to wonder about the effectiveness of that.”

After some satirical experiments with the ‘disgusting’ AI, the photographer has returned to his first love with a book of contact sheets from his celebrity shoots. ‘I wish we could go back and stop everything changing,’ he says
“I hate AI,” says Rankin . “A lot of people think I’m an evangelical twat about it, and I’m not. I think it’s disgusting. I think the people who run it are disgusting. They’ve made a massive gamble with humanity and society and culture.”
His contempt may surprise anyone who’s familiar with Rankin’s substantial AI output. Ever since the artist Damien Hirst introduced him to the possibilities of generative AI in 2021, the British photographer has been going further down the rabbit hole. “I’m not somebody who likes to be critical about something without actually knowing about it,” he explains. “I’ve gone deep into trying to work it out.”
That culminated in nine months of work for his scathing AI conceptual art project and magazine Faik (thefaik.com), made up of artificially generated images, from a skateboarding granny to Rankin-style magazine covers of the likes of Elvis, Frida Kahlo, Nelson Mandela and even God, as well as billboards with bleak warnings: “The people who control AI will control history itself”; “When anyone can generate art in seconds, who will pay for it?”
Rather than falling head-over-heels for the alluring new tech’s “limitless” possibilities, Rankin’s exploration of AI sent him running back into the arms of his first love – photography, as made by real humans in an actual time and place – and inspired his new book, Contact. “Trying to figure out what this new technology means for the craft and the thing I love reaffirmed how important the exchange between people is,” he says.
The hefty 500-plus-word page tome contains an ocean-size collection of images (bands, actors, writers, models) that Rankin took between 1987 and 2006: Oasis, Blur, Tony Blair, Kylie, Kate Moss, André 3000, Hugh Grant … Rather than presenting just the standout shot selected for a magazine cover or lead, Rankin presents contact sheets of thumbnail images, which bring to life the encounter between photographer and subject – the double meaning of the book title’s referencing the importance of human contact. “It’s about how much you kind of fall in love with people each time – platonically, of course, unless it’s my wife,” Rankin says. “I’m always going for connection. You rarely see a picture of mine where the person isn’t looking in through the camera. I tell them: ‘Forget about me – connect through the lens.’”
Born in Glasgow in 1966, Rankin, or John Rankin Waddell, grew up in St Albans, initially training in accountancy before photography consumed him. In 1991, he and Jefferson Hack co-founded the influential arts, culture and fashion magazine Dazed & Confused, Rankin’s exuberant images dominating the covers. He went on to photograph everyone from the Rolling Stones to Queen Elizabeth II. In 2011, he also founded Hunger magazine.
His next major project will be a sequel to his 2006 book Tuulitastic, dedicated to the model Tuuli Shipster, his wife of 17 years. He’s also planning to immerse himself in wet-plate photography, a slow 19th-century process that also feels like an antidote to AI.
Rankin doesn’t believe AI will replace people wanting to take or have “proper photos” taken. But he does expect it to transform the medium and devastate the industry, predicting it will be replacing jobs within less than a year, from image-retouching agencies to hair, makeup and styling. “AI is like Photoshop on crack,” he says.
While he’s not working on any AI-focused projects currently, he hasn’t finished with it entirely. “I’m quite sick of it,” he says. “But I do feel I’ve got more to explore. I’m looking at what you can create with it that you’ve never created before. People really hate it and I can’t stand it. But I’m still inquisitive about what it will become.”
Contact by Rankin is published by Hunger (£30), with a Contact exhibition also at Rankin’s Annroy Gallery , London, 2 December to3 February.
Liam and Noel Gallagher , 2002, Q , issue 190 (main image) “I always loved photographing Liam and Noel. Liam was like a panther – you never knew if he’d scratch you or purr. And Noel had brilliant one-liners. I’d set up a studio. Keith Drummond, the art director, and I were obsessed with David Bailey’s Lennon and McCartney shoot, so that inspired us. They looked so dapper, like real rock stars, and they played up the sibling rivalry for us.”
Björk , 1994, Dazed & Confused, issue 9 “Björk is the best person in the world to photograph; she’s so experimental. I was trying to do a version of another photographer’s image. She knew the photo and said: ‘Don’t do that – be yourself.’ I must’ve taken 200 rolls of film with her.”
David Bowie , 1995, Dazed & Confused, issue 14 “I expected to meet the dude from The Man Who Fell to Earth film: a spaceman who was cold, serious and unemotional. Instead, I met Tigger,” says Rankin. “Bowie was so excited. I sometimes say to people: ‘Cuddle yourself’ – it’s a self-love thing. David Bowie was one of the first people I tried it on. You can see he’s cuddling himself, but then there’s a performance there.”
Vivienne Westwood , 2002, POP magazine “Vivienne was so funny – no ego. She was such a laugh to shoot. The editor who commissioned me for this hated editing my shoots, but you can see her mark on this one. Most people would think they look ugly in that picture but Vivienne loved it so much that picture ended up being her poster for her V&A exhibition.”
Goldie , 1999, Dazed & Confused and INCredible Supplement “What’s great about Goldie is that he always performs to the camera. You never fail to get a good picture with Goldie. I like this one, as it’s a bit less like Goldie – it’s more subtle. He’s often in-your-face, which is lovely, but I feel that there’s a bit more of the softer Goldie in this photo.”

Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum has died aged 83 after a long illness.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars from King Charles to Elton John, who described Meldrum as the "single most important influence in Australian pop music".
In a statement, Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," the statement said.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.
Born in Victoria in 1943, he displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".
King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special , saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon.
"One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music. A true champion of Australian talent, you will be missed, but never forgotten."

No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia
A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.
The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government.
Initial reports said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering the explosion, the officials told the Associated Press.
Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine , marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war.
Though Ukraine began the war with no navy, it has developed a sea drone capability that threatened Russian warships in the Black Sea. The Russian fleet has been forced to retreat to the eastern port of Novorossiysk because Sevastopol in occupied Crimea had become unsafe.
Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies, the Ascalon, was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. Video showed the drone heading directly towards one end of the vessel, again causing a huge explosion.
Libyan naval forces ‌rescued the vessel’s crew, the ‌sources added. The health ministry said some crew members were in stable condition with minor injuries. The number of injured and their nationalities are not known.
Benghazi is controlled by the self-styled Libyan National Army, led by Gen Khalifa Haftar, which controls eastern and southern Libya and has been aligned with Russia.
There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range attacks against Russia far beyond the frontlines.
The UN mission in Libya (Unsmil) expressed “serious concern” over the two drone attacks off Benghazi and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”, in a post on X.
The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.
It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible.
“The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.
The specialist website Naval News earlier identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it had almost certainly been destroyed.
HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”. Similar-looking drones were involved in the subsequent attack on the Ascalon cargo ship.
If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.
But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians on another continent and the working of the port.
A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.
Russian ships regularly make use of the port, which has a growing military importance to the Kremlin, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean since the country lost its bases in Syria.
Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.
The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.
On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.
The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

A Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship Sunday at a naval base in Libya , officials said, the latest attack in the North African nation linked to the Russia-Ukraine war. A commercial vessel off the port was also hit.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday confirmed that Ukraine's military had carried out the attacks using naval drones.
The strike at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, and ignited a fire at the facility, two Libyan military officials told the Associated Press.
They said that several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, they said.
The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.
Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Muammar Gaddafi , who was later killed, in 2011. A UN-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.
Read more Russia turns to Libyan ports after Assad's ouster in Syria
The eastern Libya-based government said in a statement that the strike on Sunday caused an explosion and fire at the base, which was later extinguished.
The vessel had docked at the base for refueling and supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said, without providing details on the vessel or its cargo.
A joint investigation was launched with Russia to “uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it,” the statement said.
On Sunday evening, local media said that another sea drone hit a commercial vessel off the port of Benghazi in a separate attack.
Local officials said a "merchant vessel was targeted this evening by explosive-laden sea drones off the coast of Benghazi", but did not specify whether the ship had been Russian as well.
Reports said the second ship was sailing under a Maltese flag.
The eastern Libyan administration said all crew members had been rescued and were receiving treatment for minor injuries.
Libya Alhadath television later reported that naval and air force units intercepted more than 12 "explosive-laden sea drones" off Benghazi.
No further details were given. The Almasar satellite television channel said that naval and air forces destroyed at least 12 other sea drones off the Mediterranean city.
The western Libya government expressed concerns about “dragging Libyan ports and civilian facilities into external conflicts,” in an apparent reference to the war in Ukraine.
“The government reaffirms its categorical rejection of turning Libya into an arena for international conflicts or a theater for external powers to settle scores,” it said in a statement.
In March, Ukrainian forces operating in western Libya under a covert deal struck a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in a suspected sea drone attack near Maltese waters, Libyan officials said at the time.
The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, operated mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also at other military facilities in the capital, Tripoli, and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press.
The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".
"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X.

Democrat Chuck Hubbard was elected to the US House of Representatives from North Carolina on Sunday after defeating veteran Republican Virginia Foxx, who chairs the powerful House Rules Committee. His victory gave Democrats their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in the 2026 US midterms.
House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.
Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump ’s first midterm in 2018.
The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.
The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House . Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.
The Democrats’ majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.
“Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure,” said Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger.
“There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorized from ICE," he said earlier this month at the Capitol, referring to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "If you don't feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don't belong under this Capitol dome".
The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump.
Read more Peltola defeats Sullivan in Alaska Senate race, expanding Democratic majority
Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.
The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans’ Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.
Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.
“This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen,” said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez , D-N.Y., at the Capitol.
Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.
“Everything should be tied back to the people – and how it’s affecting the people,” he said.
For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: “How does that affect people’s pocketbooks?”
The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations – a standard oversight function of Congress – may amount to “blatant criminality”.
After House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority – meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda – the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.
Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.
"We're not a monolith – people come to the caucus with different ideas – it's OK,” said Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.
Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.
Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio , who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.
“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families,” Jordan said.
The GOP's high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

Watch: Democrat who unseated 21-year Republican incumbent says party needs to 'bring change'
The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.
The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.
Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.
Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.
"I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable.
Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".
Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."
Foxx, meanwhile, said in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."
Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of Representatives
Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.
Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.
Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.
Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.
The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.
Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.
However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

Thousands of people were evacuated from a concert in Manchester on Sunday night after an "unknown substance" was released into the crowd, police said.
The incident happened towards the end of US rapper Don Toliver's show at the Co-op Live arena at about 22:00.

Jay Clayton was pressed on Trump’s characterization of Putin during media appearances on Sunday
Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, said he trusts Donald Trump “completely” after the US president called Vladimir Putin “a friend” during their recent meeting in China.
Clayton made the remarks on Sunday, where he was pressed during media appearances on Trump’s warm characterization of the Russian president – who is viewed as a chief US adversary – following his trilateral summit with Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. After a backlash at home and aboard, Trump doubled down on Saturday and posted a photo of himself and Putin shaking hands with the caption “My Friend.”
On CNN’s State of the Union, Dana Bash asked Clayton whether he also thinks Putin is a friend to the US.
“The president is the greatest conductor of foreign policy in a very challenging time that we have seen,” said Clayton on Sunday. “Getting the three nuclear powers together and getting them to agree that they are not going to escalate, that they are going to communicate, that is historic. That is remarkable and, in that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely.”
Bash pressed on whether Clayton personally agrees that Putin should be considered a friend.
“Dana, in different contexts, you can use different words. The president pulling off that summit, getting the three of them together, is just remarkable,” Clayton replied.
Speaking with ABC’s Jonathan Karl on This Week, Clayton made similar comments, saying that “using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate” in the context of the summit.
“That conversation, that picture – historic, historic picture – was in the context of the three nuclear powers, the three main nuclear powers, getting together and saying, ‘We cannot have a nuclear incident,’” Clayton said on Sunday, referring to Trump’s post. “In that circle of that conversation, using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate.”
Clayton also dodged when asked again whether he thinks Putin should be considered a friend to the United States.
“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton responded.
Last week, Trump sidestepped questions about his views on a friendship with Putin.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said in a press briefing. “I have fantastic relationships with Putin, that’s a very good thing.”
Trump’s characterization of Putin has sparked backlash from US lawmakers and officials abroad.
“Who is he? He’s the man who has abducted tens of thousands of children, killed tens of thousands of civilians, targeted civilian infrastructure across Ukraine, detained Americans wrongfully, and continues to do so daily,” Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer posted on social media.
“Embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic,” Schumer added. “Senate Democrats will always stand with Ukraine and against Putin and autocratic dictators around the world.”
“It’s beyond me,” Senator Jeanne Shaheen said in an interview with MS NOW. “I don’t understand the president’s admiration and cozying up to Vladimir Putin, who is a war criminal.”
Trump’s comments also drew rebukes abroad, including from the deputy leader of the rightwing party Reform UK.
“It’s just wrong at every level … And it’s a grave mistake,” Richard Tice told Sky News. “He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator. And no one is in any doubt about that.”
Trump’s description of ​Putin as a friend also drew criticism from European ​allies of Ukraine. “Mr ‌Putin is ​not our ​friend and will never be,” the Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said.

“And ​as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, ⁠interruptions in service,” Clayton said on CNN’s State of the Union program. “That is ⁠going to happen.”

Indonesia has confirmed the deaths of 24 people in a fire that tore ⁠through a factory, as rescuers braved unstable structures in the burned wreckage to search for ⁠about 30 people ⁠still missing.
Authorities ​were still investigating the cause of the fire, which broke out on Saturday in the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery factory in Cikande in Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta.
Said Iqbal, ⁠a presidential adviser on labour issues, told reporters 24 people had died. He said the ​implementation of safety protocols was being ‌assessed and that he ‌would summon the factory’s chief executive.
Preliminary reports indicated the fire might have ‌been caused by an air-conditioner short circuit, Said added. The factory is owned by United Family Food, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The condition of the victims made visual identification impossible, prompting authorities to urge family members to provide DNA samples and other information that could be used to identify their loved ones, said Wahyu Hidayati Dwi Palupi, who heads the national police’s victim identification division.
She said body bags containing the remains of the victims were transferred to a hospital for identification.
The blaze had largely been contained on Sunday but firefighters were carrying out intensive cooling operations on Monday before they could access all parts of the factory, said Tubagus Mahfud, operations chief of the Serang fire department.
“We are conducting sweeps in the areas that have already been brought under control,” Mahfud said. “Parts of the structure had collapsed, while poor lighting conditions required firefighters to proceed cautiously.”
He also said the factory’s production materials could cause the fire to reignite, making it critical to complete cooling operations.
Anxious relatives have waited for news outside the burnt-out factory.
The Banten province governor, Andra Soni, said an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.
The firm employs about 5,000 people and is a major supplier of consumer goods to the domestic market. Its ‌products include Milkita, a popular confectionery brand, and Lemonilo, an instant noodle variety, according to its website.
The company’s chief executive, Steven Wijaya, said the factory regularly conducted emergency and evacuation drills in conjunction with local firefighters. Indonesia has experienced a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising concerns about workplace safety standards and emergency preparedness at manufacturing facilities.

OpenAI'ın baş bilim insanı Jakub Pachocki , yapay zeka modellerinin giderek artan yeteneklerinin beraberinde getirdiği riskleri kontrol altına almak için teknoloji şirketlerinin ortak gelişim sınırları belirlemesini önerdi. Pachocki, 22 Kasım'da yayımladığı blog yazısında , yapay zeka geliştiricilerinin modellerin davranışlarını daha iyi anlayıp denetleyebilecekleri güvenlik mekanizmaları oluşturulana kadar belirli sınırları aşmamaları gerektiğini savundu.
Pachocki'nin önerisi, yapay zekanın gelişimini tamamen durdurmayı değil, teknolojik ilerlemeyi güvenlik çalışmalarının hızına göre düzenlemeyi amaçlıyor. OpenAI CEO'su Sam Altman da Pachocki'nin gönderisinin OpenAI'ın bir süredir yayınladığı en önemli şeylerden biri olduğunu ifade ederek yazılan öneriye destek verdi .
Pachocki'nin önerisinin merkezinde, yapay zeka modellerinin performansını ölçmek için kullanılan perplexity adlı ölçüt yer alıyor. Bu ölçüt, bir modelin metindeki bir sonraki kelimeyi veya veri parçasını ne kadar doğru tahmin edebildiğini gösteriyor. Daha düşük perplexity değeri, modelin tahmin yeteneğinin daha iyi olduğu anlamına geliyor.
Pachocki'ye göre yapay zeka modellerinin belirli görevlerdeki başarısını ölçen testler, teknolojinin hızlı gelişimi nedeniyle zamanla geçerliliğini kaybedebiliyor. Perplexity ise modellerin temel eğitim sürecindeki ilerlemeyi takip etmek için daha tutarlı bir ölçüm sunabiliyor.
OpenAI, bu yaklaşımı desteklemek amacıyla modellerinin eğitim süreçlerine ilişkin daha önce kamuoyuyla paylaşmadığı bazı verileri de yayımladı. Şirketin kendi değerlendirme verilerine göre GPT-3.5'in log-perplexity değeri yaklaşık 0,99 , GPT-4' ün ise 0,91 seviyesindeydi . Değerin 0,8'in altına düşmesiyle birlikte matematik ve siber güvenlik gibi alanlarda önemli yeni yetenekler ortaya çıktı.
Pachocki, log-perplexity değerinin 0,68 ile 0,70 aralığına gerilemesiyle yeni ve önemli yeteneklerin ortaya çıkabileceğini öngörüyor. Ancak bu değerlerin henüz şirketler için belirlenmiş resmi gelişim sınırları olmadığını belirtelim.
Pachocki'nin dikkat çektiği bir diğer konu da yapay zekanın kendi gelişim sürecine katkıda bulunması oldu. Yapay zeka sistemlerinin yeni modellerin eğitim yöntemlerini geliştirmek için kullanılması, teknolojik ilerlemeyi önemli ölçüde hızlandırabilir.
Pachocki'ye göre 2027 gibi erken bir tarihte, yapay zeka modellerinin eğitimine yönelik araştırmalarda çok sayıda önemli gelişme yaşanması mümkün. Bununla birlikte güvenlik ve denetim çalışmalarının aynı hızda ilerleyemeyebileceği konusunda uyarıda bulunan Jakub Pachocki, önde gelen yapay zeka şirketlerinin ortak ölçüm yöntemleri ve gelişim sınırları üzerinde anlaşmasını arzu ediyor.
Şirketler, modellerin davranışlarını anlama ve izleme konusunda önceden belirlenmiş somut hedeflere ulaşmadan bu sınırları aşmamayı taahhüt edebilir. Ancak önerilen sistemin önünde bazı zorluklar bulunuyor. Şirketlerin farklı eğitim verileri kullanması, modellerin doğrudan karşılaştırılmasını güçleştiriyor. Ayrıca perplexity, yapay zekanın bütün yeteneklerini tek başına ölçemiyor.
Hatırlatmak gerekirse Anthropic CEO'su Dario Amodei de eylül ayında yayımladığı yazısında, yapay zeka şirketlerinin ortak güvenlik standartları oluşturmasını ve denetlenmeyen teknolojik ilerlemenin hızına sınırlar getirmesini önermişti.
OpenAI'ın yeni yaklaşımı da sektörde benzer bir iş birliğinin oluşturulmasını hedefliyor. Bununla birlikte şirketler arasında henüz ortak bir anlaşma sağlanmadığını belirtmekte fayda var. İlk gelişim sınırının hangi seviyede belirleneceği ve sistemin ne zaman uygulanacağı da şu an için bilinmiyor.

Army invokes emergency provisions in Iowa to avoid court order despite worries about health and environment risks
The US army plans to invoke emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put on hold plans to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa , saying that continued delays will make it more dangerous as the weather starts to turn colder.
“To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action,” government lawyers told the eight US circuit court of appeals in a filing late on Saturday. “Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.”
Environmental groups criticized the government’s move, decrying it as a maneuver to get around a court order and avoid public demands for safety and transparency.
The appeals court on Thursday granted a request by environmentalists to put on hold a permit that cleared the way for the detonation in Middletown, a small community about 160 miles (257km) south-east of Des Moines. It was initially planned for Friday, but the army later announced that it would push the operation to Monday after an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.
Environmentalists have called for a review of the emergency permit that was approved earlier this month by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
In a statement on Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration.
“The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm,” said Thien Chau, an attorney at Earthjustice.
Government lawyers said the army doesn’t need a permit to take emergency action against an immediate threat from explosive material.
They said the standards of a federal law regulating hazardous waste don’t apply in situations when there is an immediate threat to health, safety or the environment as determined by an explosive or munitions emergency response specialist.
Officials contend that the chemicals are unstable, and the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop. They said there is a risk that the chemicals may explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30F (-1C) in the coming days.
In March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide, which is used in munitions production. Crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.
According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums’ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.
The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their petition that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public.
Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.
Iowans in the region were told to stay inside, keep windows and doors closed, bring pets and livestock indoors, and clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces after.
“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals.”

Andy Burnham agreed a deal with the EU in Brussels on Friday
The prime minister will tell Parliament on Monday the "landmark" deal struck with the EU means there is a "very real prospect" the next decade can be "much better" than the last one.
The deal, which covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme , is a "choice between a broken status quo or change", Andy Burnham will tell MPs.
He will also call it "the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament" - repeating his claim it could add £17bn to the British economy.
But opposition parties have criticised the plan, with the Conservatives branding it unfair as UK farmers would have to follow rules made by Brussels.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
Meanwhile, the new youth experience scheme , which is due to launch no later than January 2030, will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31-year-olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.
Burnham believes the agreement reached in Brussels "holds out the very real prospect that the next decade can be a much better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through".
"The ability to draw a line on a decade of drift and division is in our hands and I believe we should take it," he will say in his speech.
He will also paint the move as a choice "between easing pressure on the cost of living or allowing food prices to rise further" and "creating opportunities for young people or denying them".
He believes polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch will use a speech at the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) annual conference on Monday to criticise Burnham's EU deal.
She will argue the prime minister should be "aiming a lot higher" on driving economic growth.
"Of course, Europe will always remain an important market. but it is not the market of the future," she will say.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage will tell the same conference that establishing closer ties with the EU would be a "disaster" for British businesses that are trying to compete and innovate.
Tories would scrap Burnham's deal with EU, deputy leader says
'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen?
On Friday, the PM said that over the coming months both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for the UK's "long-term relationship" with the EU.
He was clear that the deal he struck was "probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it".
He added: "But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."
Burnham has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.
However, he has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.
A number of former prime ministers have warned against reopening the debate over rejoining the EU.
Rishi Sunak told Sky News the issue was "divisive" and "ends up being a huge distraction for government".
Fellow Conservative former PM Baroness Theresa May told the BBC she was "aghast" Burnham could be considering rejoining the EU.
Meanwhile, former Labour PM Sir Tony Blair, who was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told the Sunday Times Britain should only rejoin the bloc if it reforms, and allows more innovation on technology.

He said the policies of ​Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich , ultra-nationalist ministers in Netanyahu's cabinet, had "brought the area to the brink of anarchy, ‌and the authorities have yet to address the crisis".
Netanyahu has not yet commented but Foreign Minister Gideon Saar condemned the attacks by a "handful of extremists" and said they are "against our values and do not represent the law-abiding citizens of Judea and Samaria", the biblical names for the West Bank.
"Israeli ‌authorities are firmly committed to enforcing the law against extremist violence," he told the ELNET Jerusalem Summit.
UN bodies and most countries of the world deny the legality of the ​settlements, which make the prospect of an independent Palestinian state ever more remote, a position Israel disputes.
Read more 'We see our culture being stolen': How Israeli settlers are attacking West Bank olive groves
Israeli police said they opened an investigation into the attacks, while the military condemned the violence, saying soldiers and police had been dispatched to the areas ​of Deir as-Sudan, Deir Abu Masha'al, Kafr Malik and At-Tuwani "following reports and footage showing vehicles being set on fire and graffiti being sprayed ​in the area".
Ben-Gvir replied in an X post that Eisenkot's condemnation amounted to selling out ​to Arab parties, which could become part of a possible new government. Smotrich favours settlement expansion and wants Israel to annex the West Bank.
Yousef Jabareen, head of the Joint List, the ​largest Arab party in Israel's parliament, said the attacks were "the direct result of the deepening occupation and a government policy under which violence against Palestinians has become an everyday occurrence", citing encouragement from Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.
Israel's parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government, after the election on October 27 stripped Netanyahu of his majority but left others with no clear path to power.
Read more Eisenkot invites Netanyahu’s party for ‘marathon’ Israeli coalition talks
President Isaac Herzog has ⁠tasked Eisenkot, who heads the centre-right Yashar, with forming a government, while Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister.
Unless Eisenkot forms a unity government with Netanyahu, he is likely to ⁠need support from Arab ​parties to be able to count on a majority of parliament's 120 seats.
If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.

US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton says Trump’s comments were ‘entirely appropriate’ in the context of the summit.
United States Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has faced pressure to justify President Donald Trump’s claims that his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin is a “friend”.
In an appearance on the ABC News show This Week, journalist Jonathan Karl pressed Clayton on Trump’s recent remarks.
“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? Because Trump said he couldn’t answer that question,” Karl asked.
Clayton responded by calling Trump’s meeting “historic” and his remarks “appropriate”, but the intelligence chief also clarified that the US has not taken Russia’s side when it comes to the country’s invasion of Ukraine.
“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton said.
The scrutiny follows a first-ever confirmed meeting between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on November 19.
The three world leaders had a roundtable on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in Shenzhen, China.
Throughout his presidency, Trump has repeatedly praised Putin. In August 2025, Trump hosted the Russian leader in Alaska for Putin’s first visit to the US in nearly a decade.
Upon reuniting with Putin at the Shenzhen conference, Trump offered him a warm, light-hearted greeting.
“Who is he?” Trump joked, first pointing to Putin, then striding across the room to shake his hand. “He’s my friend.”
Trump has since doubled down on his remarks, posting several images of their meeting on social media, one of which bore the caption , “My Friend”.
When a reporter asked whether Russia was a “friend to America” in a news briefing on Friday, Trump brushed aside the question.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said, proceeding to explain that he and Putin had grown close during an investigation into whether Russia had interfered in his favour during the 2016 US presidential election.
“I’ve been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax. And to be honest, he was very nice about it,” Trump explained.
The US State Department has long been critical of Russia over allegations of human rights abuses, including the torture and imprisonment of political dissidents.
Washington has also supported Ukraine after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, providing billions in security assistance and weaponry.
Under Trump, however, that support has cooled, with the US president openly criticising his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for failing to cut a deal with Russia.
Such remarks have divided Republicans, with critics like outgoing US Representative Don Bacon accusing Trump of “playing footsie” with Putin.
“Traditionally, Republicans stood up to Russia and China,” Bacon said last week. “We stood for freedom, and we stood up for countries that shared our values. President Trump has been terrible on this, right here.”
But in his television appearances on Sunday, Clayton defended Trump’s remarks, describing the president’s statements of friendship as “entirely appropriate” for building a personal rapport with the Russian leader.
He also praised Trump for uniting some of the world’s biggest powers for a conversation about nuclear proliferation.
“It should be assuring that you have the three world nuclear powers getting together and saying: We’re not going to go in that direction,” Clayton told This Week.
While the trilateral meeting concluded with a statement about “reducing nuclear risks”, critics point out no firm commitments were made.
Also on Sunday, in an appearance on CNN, Clayton reiterated his support for Trump’s remarks.
“In that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely,” Clayton said.

Physicians for Human Rights Israel says medics face ‘dangerous escalation’ in violence from soldiers and settlers.
Palestinian healthcare staff in the occupied West Bank are increasingly coming under attack from Israeli soldiers and settlers, according to Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI).
A report released on Monday documented a 350-percent surge in incidents involving Palestinian healthcare workers between 2022 and 2024, noting that emergency responses increasingly face assault, threats and intimidation from Israeli soldiers and settlers – even when clearly identifiable as medical staff.
As part of the report, 25 medics were interviewed, and one paramedic from the Nablus area described how Israeli soldiers prevented him from reaching a wounded man.
“I was standing close to the wounded man. I could have reached him easily, but the soldiers stopped me. He lay there bleeding until he died. Only then did they leave, and we were able to reach him,” he said.
Interviewees described physical assaults, threats at gunpoint, verbal abuse and humiliating searches. All of them said they were on edge, worried that they could be stopped, attacked or prevented from reaching patients.
“Every phone call means taking a risk. And every time I leave home, there’s a chance I won’t come back,” an ambulance driver said.
The PHRI report also documented cases where medics were forced to continue treating patients while facing threats and violence themselves.
The report author, Imran Anati, said there had been a “dangerous escalation” since October 7, 2023, when Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza started.
“These are not isolated incidents, but a systematic assault on Palestinian emergency medical care for which Israel bears responsibility,” he said.
Last year, the World Health Organization recorded 233 attacks on healthcare in the occupied West Bank, including 165 incidents affecting medical transport.
Israeli checkpoints regularly force ambulances to take long detours to reach hospitals, with some patients dying en route and pregnant women forced to give birth outside hospitals.
PHRI has previously warned that the medical system in the occupied West Bank is “collapsing”.

The US Army plans to invoke emergency powers to detonate 4 tonnes of lead azide in an Iowa town, despite a court-ordered stay.
The United States Army intends to detonate more than 4 tonnes of lead azide at a military base in Iowa, defying a federal appeals court’s order suspending its permit to do so.
In a fact sheet this weekend, the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services said that two controlled explosions were scheduled for around noon (06:00 GMT) on Monday.
That announcement follows statements from the Department of Justice, arguing that Tuesday was the cut-off date to carry out a planned detonation.
Lead azide is a key explosive used in military ammunition. The Iowa stockpile has reportedly grown unstable, and Justice Department lawyers have warned that sub-freezing temperatures could trigger an uncontrolled explosion.
“The real choice, in other words, is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion,” their court filing said.
But critics have questioned the army’s rationale for pushing ahead with the planned detonation, despite the court order to pause it.
“Anyone can claim an emergency at any point and do whatever they want. I don’t think people can or should accept that,” said Thien Chau, a lawyer with the legal group Earthjustice, which represents the plaintiffs in the lawsuit.
Chau told Al Jazeera that not enough has been done to mitigate the risk from the explosions, which are expected to release a cloud of lead into the air.
Experts say there is no safe level of lead exposure, and the dense metal can cause birth defects, brain damage and infertility.
“Anyone who hears that the army plans to explode nearly 10,000 pounds [4,500kg] of [this chemical] would recognise that that is not normal,” Chau said.
“That is extraordinary, and that is not something that you just take lightly.”
The impending explosions come after a tense legal battle between the US government and environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council.
The groups have questioned the legality of an emergency permit the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) granted on November 13. The EPA authorised the Army to move forward with the explosions, originally scheduled for November 20.
The plaintiffs pointed out that nearby residents were only given a week’s notice and that the blasts could send lead dust as far as 160km (100 miles).
They also argued that the EPA failed to properly assess safer disposal methods.
The US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit granted a pause on Friday. But in a Saturday court filing, the Justice Department maintained that the Army could still proceed with the two controlled blasts under an emergency exemption.
“The emergency exception does not depend on the Emergency Permit and is therefore not affected by, nor contradictory to, the terms of this Court’s administrative stay,” the Justice Department said in its filing.
But Earthjustice has argued that such a manoeuvre would sidestep the court’s authority.
Government lawyers have “laid the groundwork for a possible detonation without a permit, which would effectively bypass judicial process and review”, lawyer Rachel Rintelmann wrote in a Friday filing.
The controversy centres on a deteriorating stockpile of explosives stored for more than two decades at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near the city of Middletown.
The stockpile contains roughly 9,700 pounds (4.4 tonnes) of lead azide across 68 barrels, with lead accounting for approximately 6,900 pounds (about 3.1 tonnes) of its chemical mass.
The explosives had been kept in a mixture of water and ethanol to ensure their stability. But in March, military technicians at the facility discovered that the system was breaking down.
According to a court declaration , an Army munitions expert found that the liquid in the drums had evaporated, causing needle-shaped crystals to form.
That recrystallisation puts the lead azide at risk of exploding on its own, as a result of temperature charges or even friction. So many crystals had formed that it was no longer safe to even open the barrels, according to the expert.
But on Sunday, Earthjustice released a statement questioning how this problem was allowed to develop in the first place.
“This emergency is of the Army’s own making,” the statement said. “The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous. ”
The US Army has said the barrels are set to be detonated in place at the Iowa facility.
But it claims to have explored other options as well. According to the Army’s environmental assessment , it has previously considered two alternatives: chemically neutralising the explosives, or transporting them to an on-site detonation facility.
It rejected both ideas due to concerns that handling or transporting the explosives could trigger an accidental detonation.
Burying the drums, meanwhile, risked subjecting the shock-sensitive material to jolts that could similarly cause an unintended explosion.
But the health risks of even a planned explosion have put residents and environmental groups on edge.
On November 15, the Army released two plume maps outlining the potential spread of lead contamination across a swath of eastern Iowa, though projections hinge on real-time wind conditions.
The first map traces what could happen if a lead-bearing plume drifts northward, with a potential airborne trajectory over communities like Burlington, Muscatine, Davenport, Iowa City and Cedar Rapids.
The second map presents a more tenacious problem: surface exposure.
As the plume tracks north, heavier lead-bearing particles are expected to coat the landscape, landing on outdoor furniture, cars, soil and crops.
Residents in the projected plume path were advised to shelter indoors with their pets, shut windows, and limit exposure to outdoor air during a precautionary period, pending the Army’s all-clear.
Those living near Middletown City Park and Butterfly Park were also instructed to leave their homes for six hours to avoid ground vibrations that could crack or shatter nearby windows.
In the plume’s aftermath, the Army said residents would need to hose down outdoor surfaces, vehicles, and play equipment in an effort to flush away any lead dust deposited during the detonation.
But experts have expressed doubt about how practical the safety guidance is.
At a news briefing, University of Iowa professor David Cwiertny, the director of the Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination, warned that long-term monitoring would be necessary to track the lead’s distribution.
“We know that, unlike a porch or patio table, you cannot simply wipe down farm fields, gardens or topsoil because those surfaces are hard to clean,” Cwiertny said.
“We will ultimately need to rely on actual field samples after the event to measure how much lead settles there and understand what it means for our land, those crops and the quality of the environment.”
The Army has yet to issue revised instructions or specify new evacuation hours following the delayed detonation.
Earthjustice lawyers like Chau say the lack of communication is part of the problem.
“The way they’ve gone about notifying people and claiming that they’re going to clean things up when they don’t even know the extent of impact, that is extremely concerning,” Chau told Al Jazeera.
US Representative Eric Sorensen, the only meteorologist serving in Congress, said the Army should be looking at a window of opportunity that presents the least potential for off-site exposure.
In a video posted on Thursday, Sorensen said, “The most optimum conditions for controlled detonation would be when we have an inversion of clouds, warm air over cool, with light winds.”
He warned that the National Weather Service’s forecast does not offer those favourable conditions over the coming week, and he questioned why the detonations…

Virginia dinner comes as Democrats accuse president of improperly profiting from his cryptocurrency ventures
Donald Trump has headlined his third cryptocurrency gala at his ​country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin, as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profiting from his crypto ventures.
The dinner, which took place at the Trump National golf club in Sterling, Virginia, included meet-and-greets with Trump supporters including the boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, the Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary, the NBA champion Tristan Thompson and the magician Lior Suchard, according to the event’s website .
Organisers indicated that 185 crypto wallets met the criteria for Sunday’s dinner, although the leaderboard on the $Trump coin ‌club website listed just 130 wallets when the contest ‌concluded on 16 November.
Together, those listed wallets held $8.6m – a shadow of the $148m listed for the dinner in May 2025, which was attended by 220 crypto ‌investors.
A Trump fragrance, a poster, a commemorative ticket, and a watch were reserved for 120 attenders. The top 29 investors were invited to a VIP reception, and the top four received a “Trump 18K gold watch”.
Trump said his motive for supporting $Trump was to boost the economic competitiveness of the US. “I’m doing it for the United States … If we don’t do it, China’s going to do it,” he told attenders.
Participants stood in the rain as they waited to enter the venue. Attenders described the scene inside as subdued. It was a very different atmosphere to that of the first gala, when tuxedo-clad contest winners pulled up to the club in luxury sports cars, and protesters chanted and stomped outside the club as the presidential Marine One helicopter descended.
Trump has hosted two similar galas since he took office last year, bringing a flurry of criticism as Democrats accuse the president and his family of monetising his brand through an array of equities and crypto ventures while in office.
After sweeping wins in the midterms, Democrats have vowed to investigate conflicts of interest involving Trump and his personal wealth during his presidency. They also say they plan to push for legislation that would ban activities such as the meme coin gala dinners.
A letter sent by Adam Schiff and eight other US senators last month said: “This dinner and scoring mechanism appear carefully constructed to increase investment in $Trump, allowing the president to abuse the power of his office to personally enrich himself, as he has throughout this term.”
Since returning to the White House, Trump has made more than $1bn from his crypto businesses , according to financial disclosures released in June. Trump received more than $500m from his World Liberty Financial business selling new crypto products, and raked another $600m from sales of the $Trump meme coins launched days before his inauguration.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Reuters ​earlier this year: “Neither the president nor his family ⁠has ever engaged – or will ever engage – in conflicts of interest. President Trump proudly made ​the United States the crypto capital of the world ​through executive actions.”
More than half of the digital wallets publicly listed on the contest leaderboard for Sunday’s dinner were tied directly to crypto exchanges that bar US-based users, indicating they ‌are linked to foreign nationals, according to analysis of blockchain data prepared for Reuters by the nonpartisan, non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.
The Trump family ’s other crypto-connected equities and ventures have also fallen in value to record ​lows. Together, outside investors in their ‌five main crypto and ​crypto-linked projects have lost more than $5bn​, according to a Reuters analysis.
